root_cause.text: A race in the CAN ISO-TP socket teardown path lets `isotp_release()` free the potentially extended `so->tx.buf` while `isotp_sendmsg()` is still using it, because `tx.state` alone does not fully serialize buffer lifetime and `wait_event_interruptible()` can be interrupted by a signal during close.
root_cause.evidence: The patch removes `kfree(so->tx.buf)` from `isotp_release()` and adds `isotp_sock_destruct()` to free `rx.buf`/`tx.buf` at `sk_destruct` time, with the commit message explicitly stating that a signal can interrupt `wait_event_interruptible()` in `close()` while `tx.state` is `ISOTP_SENDING`, causing `release` to continue and `kfree(so->tx.buf)` while `sendmsg` may still be reading it in `isotp_fill_dataframe()`.

intent_record.intent_summary: Remove explicit RX/TX buffer freeing from ISO-TP socket release to correct teardown handling.
intent_record.what: The release path in `isotp_release()` no longer explicitly frees `so->rx.buf` and `so->tx.buf` when they differ from the embedded static buffers `so->rx.sbuf` and `so->tx.sbuf`; those `kfree()` calls were removed.
intent_record.how: At runtime, socket teardown no longer deallocates the RX and TX buffer pointers at this point in the release sequence. This changes cleanup behavior during socket release and may rely on those buffers being managed elsewhere or avoid freeing them here.

intent_record.intent_summary: Add an ISO-TP socket destructor that frees dynamically allocated RX/TX buffers during socket teardown to prevent memory leaks.
intent_record.what: A new static socket destructor function `isotp_sock_destruct(struct sock *sk)` was added. It casts the generic sock to `struct isotp_sock`, calls `can_sock_destruct(sk)`, and then conditionally frees `so->rx.buf` and `so->tx.buf` only when they differ from the embedded small-buffer members `so->rx.sbuf` and `so->tx.sbuf`.
intent_record.how: At runtime, ISO-TP socket teardown now releases any separately allocated extended RX/TX PDU buffers in addition to performing the standard CAN socket destruction. This prevents those heap allocations from being left unreleased when a socket is destroyed, avoiding memory leaks for sockets that used buffers larger than the встроенный small-buffer storage.

intent_record.intent_summary: Restore the ISO-TP socket destructor assignment during initialization so socket cleanup uses the correct destructor.
intent_record.what: In isotp_init(), after adding the socket to the notifier list and releasing the notifier lock, the code now explicitly assigns sk->sk_destruct to isotp_sock_destruct, preceded by a comment noting it re-assigns the default can_sock_destruct() reference.
intent_record.how: At runtime, ISO-TP sockets will use the protocol-specific destructor again instead of retaining the generic CAN socket destructor. This changes cleanup behavior so socket teardown follows the intended ISO-TP destruction path, preventing incorrect or incomplete resource cleanup.

bic_trace_step.reason: The shown diff is about adding configurable larger PDU buffers, not about teardown/sendmsg synchronization. In this snippet, `isotp_release()` now frees only dynamically allocated buffers: `if (so->tx.buf != so->tx.sbuf) kfree(so->tx.buf);`, while `isotp_init()` sets `so->tx.buf = so->tx.sbuf` and `so->tx.buflen = ARRAY_SIZE(so->tx.sbuf);`. The vulnerable construct described in the root cause—`isotp_release()` freeing `so->tx.buf` while `isotp_sendmsg()` is still using it because `tx.state`/`wait_event_interruptible()` do not serialize lifetime—is not shown here. There is no visible synchronization fix either (no reference counting, no close/sendmsg exclusion, no state-based lifetime protection). This commit therefore does not show the race bug itself, nor does it contain the later fix for it.
